tips.title: The front number lives between 1 and 10
tips.body: In $A \times 10^n$, **$A$ must satisfy $1 \le A < 10$**. So $12 \times 10^5$ is **not** in standard form even though it is the right size — it becomes $1.2 \times 10^6$. Checking $A$ last is the step most often skipped.

tips.title: The power counts the places the point moves
tips.body: To write a number in standard form, move the decimal point until one non-zero digit is in front of it, and **count the moves**. Moved **left**, the power is **positive**; moved **right**, it is **negative**.

tips.title: A negative power means small, not negative
tips.body: $6.2 \times 10^{-4}$ is **0.00062** — a small positive number. The minus sign is about **size**, not sign. A negative *number* in standard form carries its minus at the front: $-6.2 \times 10^4$.

tips.title: Multiply the fronts, add the powers
tips.body: Multiplying: multiply the $A$s and **add** the powers. Dividing: divide the $A$s and **subtract** them. Then check the front is still between 1 and 10 and fix it if not — that last step is where the marks go.

tips.title: Sanity-check the size
tips.body: Before writing the answer, ask roughly how big it should be. $3 \times 10^5$ is a few hundred thousand; if your answer comes out as a few hundred, a power has been lost. The order of magnitude is easier to check than the digits.

why.matters:
Some of the most useful numbers in the world are unreadable written out. The distance to a star, the mass of an atom, the number of bytes on a drive — written in full they are a wall of zeros that nobody can compare by eye.

Standard form splits a number into the two things you actually want separately: **how big it is**, which is the power of ten, and **what it is precisely**, which is the digits in front. Comparing two numbers then means comparing two small whole numbers, and multiplying them means adding those whole numbers.

That is why every calculator, every computer and every scientific instrument stores numbers this way. It is not a notation for writing things down. It is the notation for getting things done.

examples.title: A million seconds and a billion seconds
examples.body:
A million and a billion are used almost interchangeably in conversation, and they are nothing like each other.

A thousand seconds is 16.7 minutes — a coffee break. A million seconds is 11.6 days — a fortnight's holiday. A billion seconds is 31.7 years — most of a career. Each step is the same multiplication by a thousand, and only the last one feels like one.

Written out, the two differ by three easily-missed zeros in the middle of a row of them. In standard form they are $10^6$ and $10^9$, and the gap is the whole story: a factor of 1000.

This is the everyday use of the notation. Any claim about money, population or data that mixes millions and billions is asking you to compare two exponents, and the digits in front barely matter.

examples.title: How far light gets in a year
examples.body:
Light travels 299,792,458 metres every second, and that figure is exact rather than measured — the metre is defined by fixing it. A year of 365.25 days is 31,557,600 seconds.

Multiplying those two written out in full is miserable. In standard form it is one line: $3 \times 10^8$ metres per second times $3 \times 10^7$ seconds is $9 \times 10^{15}$ metres, and that is arithmetic you can do without writing anything down. Add the powers, multiply the digits.

The exact answer is $9.46 \times 10^{15}$ m, so the head estimate was within a twentieth of it. That is the real skill the notation buys: not the exact figure, but knowing **what size** the answer has to be before you reach for a calculator, so a wrong one is obvious.

examples.title: The Sun against the Earth
examples.body:
The Sun has a mass of about $1.989 \times 10^{30}$ kg and the Earth about $5.972 \times 10^{24}$ kg. How many Earths would it take?

In standard form the division is two separate, easy jobs. Divide the digits: $1.989 \div 5.972 = 0.333$. Subtract the powers: $30 - 24 = 6$. That gives $0.333 \times 10^{6}$, which tidies to $3.33 \times 10^{5}$ — about 333,000 Earths.

Notice what never happened. Nobody wrote down a number with thirty digits, and nobody lined up decimal points. The size of the answer came from the exponents and the precision came from the digits, and the two were handled separately.

That separation is the reason the notation exists, and it is why a scientist quoting a result quotes an exponent first.

steps.title: What standard form is for
steps.body:
**Some numbers are awkward to write.** The distance to the Sun is about 150 000 000 km. The width of a human hair is about 0.00007 m. Counting those zeros is slow and easy to get wrong.

**Standard form writes any number as**

$$A \times 10^n$$

**where $1 \le A < 10$ and $n$ is an integer.**

That condition on $A$ is not decoration — it is what makes the form **standard**. Every number has exactly **one** way of being written like this, so two numbers can be compared at a glance.

**Reading it.** $10^n$ says how many times to multiply by ten:

- $10^3 = 1000$, so $4.5 \times 10^3 = 4500$
- $10^{-3} = \dfrac{1}{1000}$, so $4.5 \times 10^{-3} = 0.0045$

**A positive power means a big number; a negative power means a small one.** The power is never the number of zeros — it is the number of places the decimal point moves.

**The most common error in the whole topic** is writing something like $12 \times 10^5$. The size is right, but $12$ is not between 1 and 10, so it is **not standard form**.

steps.title: Adding, subtracting and comparing
steps.body:
**Adding and subtracting is different**, and the difference catches people out. You **cannot** simply add the fronts and keep the power, because the two numbers may be different sizes.

**The safe method: make the powers the same first.**

To work out $(3 \times 10^5) + (4 \times 10^4)$:

1. Rewrite the smaller one with the **same power** as the larger: $4 \times 10^4 = 0.4 \times 10^5$.
2. Now add the fronts: $3 + 0.4 = 3.4$.
3. So the answer is $3.4 \times 10^5$.

**Alternatively, write both as ordinary numbers**, add, and convert back. On a calculator paper that is often quicker and less error-prone — and the exam does not care which route you took.

**Comparing numbers in standard form** is where the form earns its keep:

1. Compare the **powers** first. A bigger power means a bigger number.
2. Only if the powers are **equal** do you compare the front numbers.

So $2 \times 10^8$ is larger than $9 \times 10^7$, even though 9 is bigger than 2 — because $10^8$ beats $10^7$. **That works only because $A$ is always between 1 and 10**, which is the whole reason the form insists on it.

**With negative powers, remember which way the scale runs.** $10^{-6}$ is **smaller** than $10^{-3}$, so $5 \times 10^{-6} < 2 \times 10^{-3}$.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**The condition $1 \le A < 10$ is the point of the whole form.** It is what makes the representation **unique**: every number has exactly one standard form. That uniqueness is what lets you compare two numbers by looking at their **powers alone**, and it is why an answer of $12 \times 10^5$ loses a mark even though it is numerically correct — it is not *the* standard form.

**Count places, not zeros.** For whole numbers the two often agree, which is why the habit survives — but $4.5 \times 10^6$ has six places and only five zeros. On a decimal it breaks immediately: $0.00062$ has three zeros after the point and a power of $-4$. Counting the **journey of the decimal point** always works.

**Add the powers when multiplying, and always check the front afterwards.** The two-step shape — do the arithmetic, then normalise — is where the method differs from ordinary multiplication, and the second step is the one dropped under time pressure.

**Adding needs a common power first.** $(3 \times 10^5) + (4 \times 10^4)$ is **not** $7 \times 10^9$ or $7 \times 10^5$. Rewrite one so the powers match, or convert both to ordinary numbers. On a calculator paper the second route is usually faster and safer, and no marks depend on which you choose.

**A negative power means small, not negative.** $6.2 \times 10^{-4}$ is a small **positive** number. A genuinely negative number carries its sign at the front. Questions mix the two deliberately.

**Use order of magnitude as a free check.** Before writing an answer, ask roughly how big it should be. A calculation on numbers around $10^5$ and $10^7$ should land near $10^{12}$ — if it lands near $10^{2}$, a power has been dropped. Checking the **size** is quicker than rechecking the digits, and catches the errors that matter most.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Standard form is $A \times 10^n$, where **$1 \le A < 10$** and **$n$ is an integer**.
- That condition makes the form **unique**, which is what lets numbers be compared by their powers.
- To convert: move the decimal point until **one non-zero digit** is in front, and **count the places**.
- Moved **left** → **positive** power. Moved **right** → **negative** power.
- **Count places, not zeros** — $4.5 \times 10^6$ has six places and five zeros.
- A **negative power** means a **small positive** number, not a negative one.
- **Multiplying**: multiply the fronts, **add** the powers.
- **Dividing**: divide the fronts, **subtract** the powers.
- **Then check $A$ is still between 1 and 10**, and adjust the power if you fix it.
- Moving the point **one place left** adds **one** to the power.
- **Adding or subtracting**: make the **powers match** first, or convert to ordinary numbers.
- **Comparing**: compare the **powers** first; only use the fronts as a tie-break.
- With negative powers, $10^{-3}$ is **larger** than $10^{-6}$.
- **Check the order of magnitude** of any answer before writing it down.

questions.prompt: Explain what standard form is, why the front number must be between 1 and 10, and how to multiply two numbers written in it.
questions.solution:
**Standard form** writes a number as $A \times 10^n$, where **$A$ is at least 1 and less than 10** and **$n$ is an integer**. It exists because some numbers are awkward to write out: 150 000 000 and 0.00007 are both easier to read, compare and calculate with in this form.

The condition on $A$ is the part worth understanding. It makes the representation **unique**: every number has **exactly one** standard form. $12 \times 10^5$ and $1.2 \times 10^6$ are the same size, but only the second is standard form, and an answer left in the first way loses a mark despite being numerically right.

That uniqueness is not just tidiness — it is what makes the form **useful**. Because $A$ can never reach 10, it can never make up a whole power of ten, so **a larger power always means a larger number**. Two numbers can therefore be compared by looking at their **powers alone**, using the fronts only as a tie-break. $2 \times 10^8$ beats $9 \times 10^7$ even though 9 is larger than 2. Remove the condition and that shortcut collapses.

To **multiply** two numbers in standard form, **multiply the front numbers and add the powers**. For $(3 \times 10^{5}) \times (4 \times 10^{7})$: the fronts give $3 \times 4 = 12$, and the powers give $5 + 7 = 12$, so far $12 \times 10^{12}$.

The answer is not finished there, and this is where marks are most often lost. **$12$ is not between 1 and 10**, so it is not standard form. Moving the decimal point one place left turns $12$ into $1.2$ and **adds one to the power**, giving $1.2 \times 10^{13}$. Doing the arithmetic and then **normalising** is a two-step habit worth keeping, because the second step is the one dropped under time pressure.

Dividing works the same way with the operations reversed: divide the fronts and **subtract** the powers, then run the same final check.

questions.prompt: Explain why adding numbers in standard form needs a different method from multiplying them, and describe two ways of doing it correctly.
questions.solution:
When two numbers in standard form are **multiplied**, the powers are **added**. That follows from how indices work: $10^3 \times 10^5$ means three tens multiplied together times five tens multiplied together, which is eight tens multiplied together, or $10^8$. The rule is a consequence of the index law, not a convention.

**Adding is a different operation entirely, and no such rule applies.** $(3 \times 10^5) + (4 \times 10^4)$ is not $7 \times 10^9$, and it is not $7 \times 10^5$ either. The reason is that the two numbers are of **different sizes**: one is three hundred thousand and the other is forty thousand. Front numbers can only be added when they are counting the **same thing** — the same power of ten — and here they are not.

The first correct method is to **make the powers match**. Rewrite the smaller number with the larger number's power: $4 \times 10^4 = 0.4 \times 10^5$. Now both are counting hundreds of thousands, so the fronts can be added: $3 + 0.4 = 3.4$, giving $3.4 \times 10^5$. Note that $0.4$ is temporarily outside the allowed range for $A$, which is fine mid-calculation — only the **final answer** has to be in standard form, and $3.4$ is.

The second method is to **convert both to ordinary numbers**, add them, and convert back: $300\,000 + 40\,000 = 340\,000 = 3.4 \times 10^5$. On a calculator paper this is often quicker and harder to get wrong, and it doubles as a **check** on the first method. No marks depend on which route is taken.

The same reasoning applies to subtraction. And it is worth noticing what the two methods have in common: both work by making the two numbers **comparable** before combining them, which is precisely the step that multiplication does not need.

examTechnique.body:
Two habits carry this topic. First, **finish the job**: after multiplying or dividing, check the front number is still between 1 and 10 and fix it if not. Second, **count places, not zeros** when converting.

Watch for the operation. Powers **add** when multiplying and **subtract** when dividing, but adding and subtracting need the **powers made equal first** — or the numbers written out in full, which is often quicker.

examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer explains **why** $1 \le A < 10$ matters: it makes the form **unique**, which is what allows two numbers to be compared by their **powers alone**. It treats a standard form calculation as **two steps** — the arithmetic, then the normalising — and never leaves the second undone. It knows that adding requires the powers to be **made equal first**, and can say why: front numbers can only be added when they count the same power of ten. And it checks its work by **order of magnitude**, because a dropped power is far easier to spot in the size of an answer than in its digits.
